name: Cairo
tagline: Pharaohs, minarets and a city that never stops talking
description:
Cairo is loud, dusty, exhausting and utterly unforgettable — a megacity of more than 20 million where 4,500-year-old pyramids loom over apartment blocks and the call to prayer from countless minarets rolls across the rooftops at dusk. Few places on Earth let you stand before the last surviving Wonder of the Ancient World in the morning and haggle for brass lanterns in a medieval bazaar by night.

The ancient highlights are staggering: the Giza plateau and its Sphinx, the Step Pyramid at Saqqara, and the dazzling Grand Egyptian Museum, where Tutankhamun's treasures are finally displayed together. But don't skip the city's later chapters — the hilltop Citadel, the Mamluk mosques and caravanserais of Islamic Cairo, and the ancient churches of Coptic Cairo, built where tradition says the Holy Family sheltered.

Come in the cooler months, hire a good Egyptologist for the big sites, and embrace the chaos: sip sugary tea at a streetside ahwa, share a bowl of koshari with office workers, and watch the Nile turn to liquid gold from a felucca at sunset.

safety.notes: Violent crime against visitors is rare and tourist sites are heavily policed, but expect aggressive touts at Giza and Khan el-Khalili and chaotic traffic. Cross roads alongside locals and use ride-hailing apps rather than street taxis.

tipping: Baksheesh is part of daily life: add 10–15% in restaurants (the service charge rarely reaches staff), and carry small notes for guards, bathroom attendants and drivers.
gettingAround: Ride-hailing apps are cheap and far less stressful than hailing taxis, and the metro is handy for Downtown and Coptic Cairo; allow plenty of time for Giza, where traffic can stretch a 20 km trip to 90 minutes.
tips: Be at the Giza plateau when it opens at 08:00 — you'll beat the heat, the tour coaches and the worst of the touts.
Pair the Grand Egyptian Museum with the pyramids on the same day; they sit only a couple of kilometres apart on the Giza side.
Fix the price, duration, route and currency before any camel or horse ride, and pay only at the end.
Keep a stash of E£10–50 notes for baksheesh — change mysteriously becomes 'unavailable' when you hand over a large bill.
Group sights by geography: Islamic Cairo and the Citadel one day, Giza and the GEM another, Coptic Cairo and the Tahrir museum a third.
Drink bottled or filtered water and go easy on raw salads for the first few days while your stomach adjusts.
etiquette: Dress modestly, with shoulders and knees covered, especially in Islamic and Coptic Cairo; women should carry a scarf for mosques.
Remove your shoes before entering a mosque and avoid visiting during Friday midday prayers.
During Ramadan, avoid eating, drinking or smoking in public during daylight hours out of respect for those fasting.
Ask before photographing people, especially women, and never photograph police, military sites or bridges.

phrases.pronunciation: min FAD-lak (to a man), min FAD-lik (to a woman)

neighborhoods.name: Downtown (Wust el-Balad)
neighborhoods.blurb: Belle-époque boulevards around Tahrir Square, faded grand apartment blocks, cheap hostels, koshari halls and old-school cafés.

neighborhoods.name: Zamalek
neighborhoods.blurb: A leafy, upscale island in the Nile with embassies, art galleries, wine bars and many of the city's best restaurants.

neighborhoods.name: Islamic Cairo
neighborhoods.blurb: The medieval heart of the city, packed with Mamluk mosques, madrasas, monumental gates and the Khan el-Khalili bazaar.

neighborhoods.name: Coptic Cairo
neighborhoods.blurb: A walled enclave in Old Cairo holding some of Egypt's oldest churches, a historic synagogue and the Coptic Museum, all within a few quiet lanes.

neighborhoods.name: Giza
neighborhoods.blurb: The west-bank district at the edge of the desert, home to the pyramids and the Grand Egyptian Museum, with hotels boasting pyramid views.

dishes.name: Koshari
dishes.description: Egypt's national comfort food: rice, lentils, macaroni and chickpeas layered with spicy tomato sauce, garlicky vinegar and crispy fried onions.

dishes.name: Ful medames
dishes.description: Slow-cooked fava beans mashed with olive oil, cumin and lemon, scooped up with baladi flatbread — the breakfast of millions.

dishes.name: Ta'ameya
dishes.description: Egypt's take on falafel, made with fava beans instead of chickpeas — bright green with herbs inside and shatteringly crisp outside.

dishes.name: Molokhia
dishes.description: A silky, garlicky soup of finely chopped jute leaves served with rice and chicken or rabbit — divisive in texture, adored by Egyptians.

dishes.name: Om Ali
dishes.description: A warm bread-and-pastry pudding baked with milk, cream, nuts and raisins, served bubbling hot from the oven.

events.name: Coptic Christmas
events.description: On 7 January Egypt's Coptic Christians celebrate with candlelit midnight masses in the ancient churches of Coptic Cairo, followed by family feasts.

events.name: Cairo International Book Fair
events.description: One of the largest book fairs in the Arab world, drawing crowds to readings, debates and vast halls of books from late January into February.

events.name: Sham el-Nessim
events.description: An ancient spring festival shared by all Egyptians on the Monday after Coptic Easter, marked with picnics in parks and along the Nile, coloured eggs and salted fish.

events.name: Cairo International Film Festival
events.description: One of the region's longest-running film festivals fills the Cairo Opera House grounds with premieres, talks and screenings.

attractions.name: Pyramids of Giza
attractions.description: The Great Pyramid of Khufu, raised some 4,500 years ago from more than two million limestone blocks, is the only Ancient Wonder still standing, flanked by the pyramids of Khafre and Menkaure. Walk the perimeter, peer into a noble's tomb, then head to the desert-side panorama point for the classic all-nine-pyramids shot.
attractions.bookingTip: One ticket covers the plateau; going inside the Great Pyramid costs extra and daily numbers are limited, so buy it right at opening.

attractions.name: Great Sphinx of Giza
attractions.description: Carved from a single limestone outcrop, the lion-bodied Sphinx with a pharaoh's face has guarded the plateau for more than four millennia. The terrace beside Khafre's Valley Temple gives the classic face-on angle with the pyramids rising behind.
attractions.bookingTip: Access is included in the Giza plateau ticket, so visit straight after the pyramids and skip anyone selling separate 'Sphinx tickets'.

attractions.name: Grand Egyptian Museum
attractions.description: The world's largest museum devoted to a single civilisation greets you with a colossal statue of Ramesses II and a monumental staircase lined with pharaohs, leading to galleries where Tutankhamun's entire tomb collection is shown together for the first time. Vast windows frame the pyramids just down the road.
attractions.bookingTip: Book timed tickets on the official website and budget at least half a day — the Tutankhamun galleries alone deserve two hours.

attractions.name: Egyptian Museum
attractions.description: The rose-coloured 1902 museum on Tahrir Square is a gloriously old-fashioned treasure house, crammed with statues, sarcophagi, papyri and jewellery spanning thousands of years in wooden cases that feel unchanged for a century. With many headline pieces moved to the GEM, it's calmer, quirkier and still richly rewarding.
attractions.bookingTip: Hire a licensed guide at the entrance for an hour — labelling is sparse, and a good guide brings the collection to life.

attractions.name: Saqqara
attractions.description: Home to Djoser's Step Pyramid, the oldest monumental stone building in Egypt, this sprawling necropolis also hides nobles' tombs whose painted scenes of fishing, farming and feasting are still vivid after four millennia. It's far quieter than Giza and endlessly atmospheric.
attractions.bookingTip: Hire a driver for the day and combine it with Dahshur's Bent and Red Pyramids — public transport reaches neither site.

attractions.name: Khan el-Khalili
attractions.description: A 14th-century bazaar that still hums with trade, its alleys glittering with brass lanterns, perfume bottles, spices and silver. Duck into a centuries-old coffeehouse for mint tea while street musicians and hawkers drift past.
attractions.hours: Roughly 10:00–late daily; some shops close for Friday prayers and on Sundays
attractions.bookingTip: Come after dark when the lanterns glow and local families arrive, and wander the side alleys where workshops still make what's sold.

attractions.name: Al-Azhar Mosque
attractions.description: Founded in 970, Al-Azhar is among the oldest continuously working mosques and centres of learning in the world, its gleaming marble courtyard ringed by minarets added across many dynasties. Visitors are welcome outside prayer times, and the calm is a striking contrast to the bazaar outside.
attractions.hours: Open daily outside prayer times; closed to tourists during Friday prayers
attractions.bookingTip: Women should bring a headscarf and everyone removes shoes at the door; a small tip for the shoe attendant is customary.

attractions.name: Cairo Citadel
attractions.description: Salah al-Din's medieval hilltop fortress is crowned by the Ottoman-style Mosque of Muhammad Ali, whose silvery domes and pencil-thin minarets dominate the skyline. The terrace alongside offers a vast panorama over a sea of minarets — on clear days all the way to Giza.
attractions.bookingTip: Go early on a clear winter morning for the best chance of spotting the pyramids from the terrace.

attractions.name: Al-Azhar Park
attractions.description: Built over a centuries-old rubble mound, this beautifully landscaped park of fountains, palms and terraced gardens offers the finest sunset view over Islamic Cairo's domes and minarets. It's a favourite with Cairene families and courting couples on warm evenings.
attractions.bookingTip: Arrive an hour before sunset and grab a terrace table at one of the park's cafés for the golden-hour skyline.

attractions.name: Hanging Church
attractions.description: Perched above the gatehouse of a Roman-era fortress, this Coptic church is reached by a steep stair and filled with cedar-and-ivory screens and centuries-old icons. It's the jewel of Coptic Cairo, a walkable enclave of churches, a synagogue and the excellent Coptic Museum.
attractions.hours: 09:00–16:00 daily; services on Friday and Sunday mornings
attractions.bookingTip: Take the metro to Mar Girgis station, which drops you right beside the enclave's entrance.

hotels.name: Qasr al-Nakheel Nile Palace
hotels.description: A 1920s palace on the Nile Corniche restored with marble floors, mashrabiya screens and suites whose balconies hang over the river. The rooftop pool and hammam spa are a blissful escape from Downtown's traffic.

hotels.name: Beit el-Sukkar
hotels.description: Ten rooms in a restored Ottoman-era house a short walk from the bazaar, with carved wooden screens, stained-glass windows and a rooftop overlooking a forest of minarets. The owners arrange walks with a local architectural historian.

hotels.name: Balcona Downtown Hostel
hotels.description: High-ceilinged dorms and private rooms on the upper floors of a belle-époque block near Tahrir, reached by a gloriously creaky antique cage lift. The balcony lounge looks down on Downtown's buzzing streets.

hotels.name: Akhet Design Hotel
hotels.description: Sandstone, brass and clean-lined furniture echo ancient Egyptian geometry in this sleek hotel near the GEM, where many rooms and the rooftop pool frame the pyramids. The lobby showcases work by contemporary Egyptian designers.

hotels.name: Dar Khafre Rooftop Rooms
hotels.description: A family-run guesthouse steps from the Sphinx gate, with simple, spotless rooms and a rooftop terrace where breakfast comes with a front-row view of the pyramids. After dark you can watch the sound-and-light show from your chair.

hotels.name: Bayt al-Mashrabiya
hotels.description: A Mamluk-era courtyard house beneath the Citadel walls, restored by local craftsmen with carved wooden screens, marble fountains and antique brass lamps. It's a peaceful base for exploring historic Darb al-Ahmar on foot.

restaurants.name: Koshari Nagah
restaurants.description: A bustling multi-storey koshari hall where waiters sling metal bowls of rice, lentils and pasta at lightning speed. Customise it with extra fried onions, chilli oil and garlicky da'ah vinegar — and don't be shy with the hot sauce.

restaurants.name: Ahwa el-Fanous
restaurants.description: Mirrored walls, brass trays and wicker stools spill into a bazaar alley at this atmospheric ahwa, where waiters juggle mint tea, thick Turkish coffee and creamy sahlab. Stay late for the oud player and the people-watching.

restaurants.name: Am Hosny's Fuul Cart
restaurants.description: Every morning Am Hosny wheels his copper fuul urn to the same corner near Mar Girgis station, ladling slow-cooked fava beans and stuffing hot ta'ameya into baladi bread. Breakfast for two costs less than a coffee back home.
restaurants.signatureDish: Ful medames with a ta'ameya sandwich

restaurants.name: Khepri Tasting Room
restaurants.description: A glass-walled dining room facing the pyramids, where a young chef reinvents Egyptian home cooking — molokhia as a jade-green velouté, pigeon stuffed with freekeh, Om Ali as a feather-light soufflé. It's licensed, with Egyptian wines or a hibiscus-and-tamarind alcohol-free pairing.

restaurants.name: Kababgi Abu Seif
restaurants.description: A smoke-filled grill house below the Citadel serving kofta, lamb chops and grilled quail by the kilo with tahini, pickles and puffy baladi bread. It has fed the neighbourhood's butchers and bus drivers for decades.
restaurants.signatureDish: Mixed kofta and kebab by the kilo

restaurants.name: Sofret Teta
restaurants.description: Grandmother's recipes served in a tiled dining room near Al-Azhar: fragrant molokhia, stuffed vine leaves, fatta drenched in garlic vinegar and Om Ali straight from the oven. Ask for the day's mahshi platter.

restaurants.name: Beit Zaatar
restaurants.description: A leafy garden terrace with a pyramid view, turning out Lebanese mezze — smoky moutabal, herb-packed tabbouleh, za'atar manakish — and charcoal-grilled shish taouk. A relaxed lunch after a morning on the plateau.

restaurants.name: Saqqara Palm Grove Kitchen
restaurants.description: Under date palms beside an irrigation canal, a farming family serves roast duck, stuffed pigeon and feteer baked in a clay oven. It's a peaceful, very local lunch stop between the pyramids of Saqqara and Dahshur.

experiences.name: Pyramids at Opening with an Egyptologist
experiences.description: Arrive as the gates open with a university-trained Egyptologist who explains how — and why — the pyramids were built, then circle the plateau to the Sphinx and Khafre's Valley Temple before the crowds build. Entry inside the Great Pyramid can be added.

experiences.name: Saqqara and Dahshur Tombs Day Trip
experiences.description: Explore the Step Pyramid complex and the painted tombs of Saqqara, then continue to Dahshur to clamber inside the Red Pyramid and admire the oddly angled Bent Pyramid, often with barely another visitor in sight. Lunch is at a village restaurant among the palms.

experiences.name: Islamic Cairo After-Dark Street-Food Walk
experiences.description: Follow a Cairene foodie through the lanes around Al-Muizz Street, sampling hawawshi, feteer, spicy liver sandwiches, roasted sweet potatoes and syrupy basbousa, with a tea stop at a historic coffeehouse. Floodlit mosques and gates make the route magical.

experiences.name: Nile Felucca Sunset Sail
experiences.description: Drift along the Nile on a traditional wooden felucca as the city lights flicker on and the call to prayer echoes from both banks. Your captain steers by wind alone while you settle into the cushions.
